the intended spelling from the helper or variable name alone.

compatibility.

or unsupported claims and distinguish source inspection from execution.

reads. Check every tensor name the code requests, including alternate and optional names, against the names in
the header, and say which are absent and which path the code then takes. Do not describe tensor layout as
unestablished while headers are available and unread.

      "content": "Summary: Swapped out original LCG params in 3INST for a better, computationally screened, optimal MCG multiplier\r\n\r\n0.2-3.9% lower PPL\r\n1.25% faster processing (addition removed)\r\n\r\n\r\nDetails:\r\n\r\n3INST's default LCG params are knowably suboptimal:\r\nx = 89226354 * x + 64248484\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\n| Property | 89,226,354 (0x5517C72) | 4,286,219,237 (0xFF7A83E5) |\r\n|----------|-------------------|----------------------|\r\n| Odd | \u274c | \u2705 |\r\n| >sqrt(2^32) | \u2705 | \u2705 |\r\n| >2^32/2 = 2147483648 | \u274c | \u2705 |\r\n| Congruent 5 (mod 8) | \u274c | \u2705 |\r\n| High figure of merit | \u274c | \u2705 |\r\n| \"Spectrally good\" in higher dimensions | \u274c | \u2705 |\r\n| Maximum potency | \u274c | \u2705 |\r\n\r\n\r\nSee [Computationally easy, spectrally good multipliers for congruential pseudorandom number generators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.05304) for deeper discussion\r\n\r\nDemanding LCGs have good spectral properties is not always necessary but for a 256-diminsion Trellis Decoder, spectral quality in higher dimensions is actually a key performance requirement.\r\n\r\nScreened all 45458 spectrally good LCG multipliers and all 49507 spectrally good MCG multipliers [uploaded to github](https://github.com/vigna/CPRNG) by @vigna\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\nMany LCG multipliers had strictly lower RMS in the decoder but none had universally superior PPL when actually quantizing and decoding real models.\r\n\r\nBut several MCG multipliers had both lower RMS in a vacuum AND universally better PPL on several models @ multiple bitrates. The best one appears to be 0xFF7A83E5.\r\n\r\n![0xff7a83e5_codebook](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6d36f1e7-f4f1-4ce4-9407-155faba0f328)\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\n### Performance Comparison of Multiplier 0xFF7A83E5 Across Models\r\n\r\n| **Metric** | **Mistral-7B-instruct** | **Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct** |\r\n|------------|-------------------------|---------------------------|\r\n| **Original Baseline (89226354)** |  |  |\r\n| Baseline PPL@2.00 | 6.897755 | 23.382405 |\r\n| Baseline PPL@3.00 | 5.962067 | 15.637272 |\r\n| Baseline PPL@4.00 | 5.821786 | 14.540853 |\r\n| **With Multiplier 0xFF7A83E5** |  |  |\r\n| PPL@2.00 | 6.881336 | 22.464554 |\r\n| PPL@3.00 | 5.957563 | 15.410229 |\r\n| PPL@4.00 | 5.820617 | 14.468759 |\r\n| **Improvement (%)** |  |  |\r\n| Imp@2.00 | 0.238% | 3.93% |\r\n| Imp@3.00 | 0.076% | 1.45% |\r\n| Imp@4.00 | 0.020% | 0.50% |\r\n| **Overall Performance** |  |  |\r\n| Avg Improvement | 0.111% | 1.96% |\r\n| Total Improvement | 0.334% | 5.87% |\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\nAlso inspected how this impacts the CUDA (removing addition):\r\n\r\nOriginal CUDA PTX:\r\nmad.lo.s32 \t%r4, %r3, -1997118179, 64248484;\r\nand.b32  \t%r5, %r4, -1879076865;\r\nxor.b32  \t%r2, %r5, 996162400;\r\n\r\nNew CUDA PTX:\r\nmul.lo.s32 \t%r4, %r3, -8748059;\r\nand.b32  \t%r5, %r4, -1879076865;\r\nxor.b32  \t%r2, %r5, 996162400;\r\n\r\n\r\nBenchmarking reveals small but measurable 1.25% speed increase by eliminating addition.\r\n\r\nEven modest 1.25% speedup and a small 0.2-3.9% lower PPL is hard to come by in other places, given how efficient EXL3 is shaping up to be.",

      "content": "More evidence for 0xFF7A83E5\r\n--\r\nOut of curiosity, I coded my own routines to reproduce the QTIP paper's distortion rate calculations.\r\n\r\nGot slightly different results than what they reported:\r\n\r\n|                   | **My tests** | **QTIP** | **Difference** |\r\n|-------------------|--------------|----------|----------------|\r\n| LLOYD-MAX         | 0.1172       | 0.118    | 0.7%           |\r\n| 1MAD              | 0.0687       | 0.069    | 0.4%           |\r\n| DR(infinite)      | 0.0625       | 0.063    | 0.8%           |\r\n| 3INST             | 0.0743       | 0.069    | 7.7%           |\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\nFirst 3 are nitpicks... essentially just replicating their work with 1 more sig fig.\r\n\r\n* Although, I'll note others have also published 0.0117 as the distortion rate for 2-bit Lloyd-Max\r\n* DR (infinite) = 2^(-2 * bitrate) = 2^(-2 * 2) = 2^-4 = 0.0625.     {
      "author_login": "meigami0",
      "content": "I encountered a VRAM allocation issue while testing exllamav3 quantized models with TabbyAPI. Even with ~1GB VRAM remaining, the system throws an error: `RuntimeError: Insufficient VRAM in split for model and cache`. Below are test results for two models on 24564MiB VRAM (RTX4090):  \n\n#### Model 1: **Nemotron-Super-49B** (3.0bpw, `cache-mode FP16`)  \n- 2k context: 19162MiB used  \n- 12k context: 21342MiB used  \n- 20k context: 23094MiB used  \n- 21k context: 23194MiB used  \n- 22k context: OOM  \n\n#### Model 2: **gemma3-27b** (5.0bpw, `cache-mode Q6`)  \n- 2k context: 17404MiB used  \n- 12k context: 19404MiB used  \n- 22k context: 21660MiB used  \n- 30k context: 23238MiB used  \n- 31k context: OOM  \n\nEnvironment: WSL Ubuntu+Python12+torch2.7.0+cu128+exllamav3-0.0.3+tabbyAPI default config\n\n**Questions:**  \n- Is this behavior expected under exllamav3\u2019s current memory management design?  \n- Are there recommended configurations or workarounds to better utilize the remaining VRAM?",
      "content_sha256": "38c73221713b41d0e3eb99acbaccdcbf2e804689c2fdbf9d48e8726b20590df7",
      "created_at": "2025-06-09T10:03:09Z",
      "representation": "body",

      "source_id": "I_kwDOOU24Gs66jTPW",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/50"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "turboderp",
      "content": "A couple of likely contributing reasons:\n\nMomentary VRAM allocations can be so quick that they don't show up in a monitoring utility which might be polling, say, once per second. So if you see:\n     \n- 20k context uses 23.1 GB, and\n- 21k context uses 23.2 GB, so you might expect\n- 22k context uses 23.3 GB, but..\n\n... this might not be accounting for 0.75 GB of temporary storage for some large operation that's too fast to notice.\n\nThe reason you might get this OoM error while loading is that the model performs a dummy forward pass as it shovels tensors onto the GPU, to determine precisely where the overflow occurs and thus where it should split the model in a multi-GPU setup.\n\nThis inference-while-loading can make it look like the model needs more VRAM as it's loading than it does afterwards. Really it's just accounting for the worst case while loading. The chunk size is adjustable in Tabby's config if you want a different worst case. Smaller chunk size reduces the overall VRAM requirement somewhat but also makes prefill somewhat slower. Tabby's default is 2048.\n\nAlso, by default a small buffer amount is reserved on each GPU to keep things stable, especially for the first GPU which might also be running a desktop environment. You can change the size of this reserve in Tabby's config, or if you're calling ExLlama directly, there are arguments to the `load()` and `load_gen()` functions.\n\nIn multi-GPU splits, ExLlama only splits whole layers. So if each of your devices would fit 12.7 layers in theory, you end up with 12 layers on each and 0.7 layers worth of unused memory.\n\nFinally, VRAM fragmentation is a thing and is not accounted for by `nvidia-smi`. Having 23.5 GB free on a 24 GB device doesn't mean you can allocate an extra block of 0.5 GB tensor somewhere.",

I've seen even 98% before.\n\n",

    {
      "author_login": "Ph0rk0z",
      "content": "k, I dived into the code and what it's doing.\n\nThe allocator takes some baseline + usage and converts it into a fraction of total GPU memory as reported by pytorch. 23.59 gets you to the maximum. It's basically gpu_split * 1024/free mem, which is why it doesn't match what I requested.\n\nTorch for some reason only allows 23798, maybe due to overhead? In either case, the fractions were 1.0 and it still wasn't using the whole thing and going OOM early.\n\nSearching around I found `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True`\n\nAfter setting this, suddenly there is a whole lot of free memory, one GPU is in the 70s even with 32k context. Dunno what it does to cuda malloc, but for now it seems to have solved the issue. Model load no longer fails. Don't remember having to do this previously or getting anything back from it.",
      "content_sha256": "d6b4452cc03c48a1c2254e2a07a59fab7cc162387bea454acf0766f512a37ebd",
      "created_at": "2025-06-19T18:28:36Z",

      "source_id": "IC_kwDOOU24Gs6yJm6c",
      "url": "https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav3/issues/54#issuecomment-2988863132"
    },
    {
      "author_login": "turboderp",
      "content": "EXL3 doesn't statically allocate all the memory it needs for inference. While loading it runs a worst-case forward pass to know when to split layers so as to make sure inference will subsequently work, but it doesn't hold on to that memory after the model is loaded. Among other things, this allows for a vision and text model to share the same dynamic memory since they won't be running concurrently anyway. It may leave memory seemingly unused when you're forwarding one token at a time, but since that memory is accounted for while loading it prevents OoM errors when you later want to process a prompt in 2048-token chunks. If that's not a situation you care about you can reduce the max chunk size and reserve less memory, but then you'll also have slower prompt processing as a tradeoff.\n\nIt's not always possible to reach 100% utilization on each GPU regardless, though, since the model is split into whole layers. Each layer on Qwen3-235B is about 2.5 billion params, so even at 2 bpw that's a 600 MB chunk of weights (plus 1/94 of the KV cache) that resides either on CUDA:0 or CUDA:1, making it difficult to achieve a split that hits exactly 99.9% VRAM usage. But that's not necessarily something you'd want to aim for anyway, any more than you'd want to use 99.9% of your system RAM or your disk space at all times. A little bit of headroom is a good thing.\n\n`expandable_segments` changes the behavior of Torch's caching allocator, possibly leading to less fragmentation, but in other cases potentially hurting performance. It's something you can try but not really something I can test and document. More along the lines of \"maybe try a different driver version and see what happens.\" :shrug:\n\nMain point though is that EXL3 uses dynamic allocations in some places where EXL2 uses static allocations. Just because usage is sitting at 93% after loading doesn't mean it won't jump to 99% momentarily if you feed it a long prompt.",

    },
    {
      "author_login": "Ph0rk0z",
      "content": "I'm going to try long prompts on it and see what happens (maybe even 4096 batch). Speed actually increased by .20 t/s. I thought that tabby attempts to test full context length when loading but could be wrong. \n\nSmells like we're bitten by pytorch here again. You use the native functions for memory, something like llama.cpp uses C.
